name: Maya Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'll tell you what, my days are pretty plain. I buy hand tools, garden supplies, paint and household goods for Ridgeway Hardware Supply in Millford. It's a family firm, started by old Mr Ridgeway's father, and I've been there fourteen years. I go through the catalogue, call my reps and haggle on every order. I drive out to the yard twice a week to look at what we're really holding. I like that people know my voice and that a handshake still counts. What wears me out is that the big chains squeeze us every year, and my pay is lower than it should be after fourteen years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good. Let people use computers for the dull bits, and let the rest of us get on. At church I'd say we've been told the sky is falling a dozen times. At work I'd say nothing, because I've never used any of those tools and I don't plan to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's a relief, but I'm not settled. We have a mortgage, Hannah is twelve and Caleb is nine, and less than a month saved. Daniel is a roofer, which is good steady work, but in winter the jobs dry up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do. I'd cut where we can, make the cheap meals, and keep the car another two years. I'd talk with Mr Ridgeway about where the firm stands, because the big chains are eating his customers and I'd like to know before I'm told.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but tight. I'd say grateful for the work. I'm not asking for much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In a world where AI changes little, what weighs on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January, when the roofing slows, we live on my wage alone. That wage barely covers the mortgage and the food. If Ridgeway lost two accounts to the chains, I'd be looking at cuts. That's my worry, not the computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is Ridgeway doing against the big chains?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the government to leave small firms alone: less paperwork and fewer rules that only a big chain can follow. And I'd want the chains to stop dumping stock below cost. We can't compete with that.

say: I'd say **good**; let computers do the dull bits and the rest of us get on.
At church I'd say we've heard the **sky is falling** many times.
think: I'm relieved but **not settled**; the mortgage and under a month saved weigh on me.
In January, when roofing slows, we live on **my wage alone**.
do: Keep doing the job and **cut** where we can.
Keep the old car **another two years**.
Ask Mr Ridgeway **where the firm stands**.
feel: **Steady but tight**, grateful for the work.

fieldNote: The real worry is her family firm losing accounts to **big chains**, not AI.
Her husband's **seasonal roofing** leaves winters on her wage alone.
Free-market view: wants **fewer rules** for small firms and no dumping by chains.

steps.text: Keep the car another two years and skip the new tyres
Ask Mr Ridgeway how the firm stands against the chains
Keep buying from the same reps and the same yard

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario two is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that people will adapt, as they always have. At church I'd say we should look after our own: neighbours, family and the folks who lose out. And I'd say it's not government's job to fix everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. Half of what I do is checking orders and prices, which is on that list. I've never used any of those tools and I'm not quick at new things. If the firm buys a system, I'm not sure they'd teach me, or keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Ridgeway to put me on whatever training he buys, even if I'm not keen. I'd save as much as I could and cut the extras. And I'd lean on the part that's still personal: the reps and the yard, where I know every shelf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, tipping into worried. I don't like being rushed into new tools by people who don't know my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks might software take, and which would you keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reorders and price checks go first. The reps and the old customers who call me stay with a person. I'd hold on to those and tell myself they're enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Ridgeway would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young girl in the office, Brittany, who does all our invoices. And the two of us in buying, me and Walt, who's sixty-two. I'd worry about Walt because he's near the door anyway. I'd worry about myself because I'm slower than I used to be at screens.

say: I'd say people **adapt**, as they always have.
I'd say we should look after our own, and it's **not government's job** to fix everything.

Lean on the **reps and the yard**, where I know every shelf.
feel: **Uneasy**, tipping into worried; I dislike being rushed.

fieldNote: She admits **slowness with screens** but plans to learn if the firm pays.
Values **personal relationships** with reps and the yard.
Worries about an **older colleague** and herself.

steps.text: Ask Mr Ridgeway to put me on the reorder software training
Cut the extras and save fifty a week
Keep the rep calls and the monthly yard count as my own work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario three is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and nobody has asked ordinary families if they want this. I'd tell people at church to lean on each other. And I'd say the people building it should answer for what happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened. If a machine can do any thinking work, my work is gone, and so is Ridgeway's need for a buyer. We have no cushion. Our family is a paycheck and a half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Pastor Elias and my sister about what help is out there. I'd cut every cost I can. Daniel would take every roofing job he can find, even in the cold. And I'd ask around about work in the yard or on the road, because I don't think those go as soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd pray a lot, and I'd still lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What would you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would be a different story. I could train or save, or ask the kids to learn a trade. With two years, I have to keep my head down and hold on to the job as long as I can. And I'd need people to hold me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is mostly desk and phone, with yard visits. How do you see robots coming three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots coming later is some comfort, because Daniel's roofing is hands-on and holds up longer than my desk job. But roofing can't pay for the whole house. Three extra years for my husband is good, though I'd still be out first.

I'd say the people building it should **answer** for what happens.
think: If a machine can do any thinking work, my work is **gone**.
We have no cushion; our family is a **paycheck and a half**.
do: Talk to **Pastor Elias** and my sister about help.
Cut **every cost** I can and have Daniel take every roofing job.
Ask about **yard or road** work that lasts longer.
feel: **Alarmed**; I'd pray a lot and still lie awake.
S2.quote: Three extra years for my husband is good, though I'd still be out first.
fieldNote: She blames the **people building AI**, not government or the firm.
Her **husband's roofing** gives the family three extra years.
Leans on **faith and church** for support.

steps.text: Talk to Pastor Elias and my sister about what help exists
Cut the budget to rent, food and the mortgage only
Ask about yard and delivery jobs that last longer
Have Daniel take every roofing job through the winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario four is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is some time, and people should use it to get ready and not to complain. I'd say the schools should teach trades again. At church I'd say, don't wait for anyone to hand you something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm still alarmed but less so. A few years lets me do something. I'm not good with new tech, but I'd have time to be bad at it for a while. The thing I fear is being too proud to ask for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save more than I think I can, even if it's twenty a week. I'd ask Mr Ridgeway for any training he can give, and maybe learn the basics of the reorder tool. And I'd look at jobs in the yard, or in supervising people, where a person is still needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I'd be in motion, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What do you do in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn a trade they could be proud of, and to learn to work with people. Hannah's good with her hands, Caleb's good with numbers. I'd tell them both that a good name and a good skill matter more than a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hannah and Caleb?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The year after it arrives would matter more than the year before it. I'd want to keep Daniel on the roofs and keep us out of debt. If I lose the job, he can carry us a while, at least until about 2034.

say: I'd say five years is some time; **get ready** and don't just complain.
I'd say schools should teach **trades** again.
think: I'd be alarmed but **less so**; I could be bad at the tools for a while.
I fear being **too proud** to ask for help.
do: Save **twenty a week**, more than I think I can.
Ask Mr Ridgeway for **training** and learn the basics of the reorder tool.
S3.quote: I'm not good with new tech, but I'd have time to be bad at it for a while.
fieldNote: Pride is her **real obstacle**, and she says so.
Wants her children in **trades** and good with people.
Counts on **Daniel's** hands-on work to carry the family.

steps.text: Save twenty a week in a separate account
Learn the basics of the reorder tool on Friday afternoons
Apply for yard supervisor roles at Ridgeway and nearby
Plan Hannah's school years around a trade apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario five is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off, and it will sort itself out as it always has. I'd tell the young folks to learn trades. At church I'd say hold on to the old ways of looking after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's a lot of time but it doesn't feel safe. By 2036 I'm fifty-three. I could still be working fourteen years from then. So I'd rather prepare a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and pay down the mortgage as best I can. I'd try the reorder tool when they bring it, and ask for a bit of training. And I'd look at managing the yard in a few years, since the yard needs a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady. A little dull worry, like a cough you don't think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, does this still touch you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Ridgeway to be honest about the firm's plans. And I'd say at church that we should keep a fund for families who lose work. People here would give, if somebody organised it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the long wait change what you'd say to the owner or the church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ten years help me, but it's the money that decides. A decade of mortgage payments and school costs comes first. I'd like to have six months saved by 2030.

I'd tell young folks to **learn trades**.
think: By 2036 I'm fifty-three, with many working years left, so it **doesn't feel safe**.
I'd rather **prepare** a bit than be caught out later.

S4.quote: A decade of mortgage payments and school costs comes first.
fieldNote: Money keeps her **anxious** even with a long runway.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's no time and no cushion. What would help is honest talk from the owner, a firm that gives notice, apprenticeships and training that lead to real work. And church and neighbours helping each other, which I think is better than a government form. But a bit of help for the short term wouldn't hurt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that I'm not against progress. I just think the people who build these things should carry the cost, and the rest of us shouldn't be left to pick up the pieces. And I'd like my kids to have a good skill, not just a screen.

headlineQuote: I'm not against progress. I just think the people who build these things should carry the cost, and the rest of us shouldn't be left to pick up the pieces.
portrait: **Maya Young**, 43, buys hardware for Ridgeway Hardware Supply in Millford, on **lower pay** with under a month saved.
Her **husband Daniel** is a roofer with slow winters; they have two children and a mortgage.
She has **never used AI**, likes handshakes and faith-based community help, and distrusts handouts.
Her mood stays **anxious** to **alarmed**, with money and the family firm worrying her more than robots.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because there's no cushion and no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest** notice from the owner, **apprenticeships**, and neighbours and church helping each other.
